1-over-the-moon::0.title: Over the moon
1-over-the-moon::0.snippetHtml: On April 13, 1970, an oxygen tank exploded on the service module of Apollo 13. So instead of orbiting and landing on the moon as planned, they precariously set themselves up to sling around it and back to Earth on a free return trajectory.

1-over-the-moon::1.title: Over the moon
1-over-the-moon::1.snippetHtml: Today, after 53 years of lunar unadventure, the Artemis II mission is scheduled to launch. Unlike all the other Apollo missions that flew to the moon but did not land, Artemis II will not orbit. It’ll do a free return. Planned, this time.

1-over-the-moon::2.title: Over the moon
1-over-the-moon::2.snippetHtml: Yesterday, I left Montréal and arrived at Lighthaven to participate in Inkhaven. One short hop to Toronto, one six-hour flight to SFO, one hour-and-some BART ride to Berkeley. This presented somewhat less of a legroom problem than spending 10 days in space, tinned and ballistic.

1-over-the-moon::3.title: Over the moon
1-over-the-moon::3.snippetHtml: Among other things, astronauts are chosen for their exceptional stability. They need to execute complex and repetitive procedures for hours, and make only minimal, recoverable errors. Preferably no errors. When an accident happens, they need to keep performing. They must not be overcome by fear. To an astronaut, panic is not just a sense of impending doom. It is impending doom.

1-over-the-moon::4.title: Over the moon
1-over-the-moon::4.snippetHtml: I’m used to being scared, so it comes as a mild surprise to find I am not, now that I’m here. Actually I'm rather elated. What’s different from my visit to Lighthaven last June? I was much more nervous then...

1-over-the-moon::5.title: Over the moon
1-over-the-moon::5.snippetHtml: Maybe it’s that this trip has more of a coherent intention behind it. Or, that the small-ish size of the cohort means there’s less prospect of interacting with an endless stream of strangers, than at Manifest.

1-over-the-moon::6.title: Over the moon
1-over-the-moon::6.snippetHtml: Maybe it’s because I did some squats in the gym this morning. Or, that I no longer drink any alcohol. Or that I’m finally able to keep to no more than 50 mg of caffeine per day, no matter any naive impulse to grab for more of its frenetic energy, and pay the tiresome price when it wears off.

1-over-the-moon::7.title: Over the moon
1-over-the-moon::7.snippetHtml: Maybe it’s that I was in a good mood last night, and set the stage with a couple of easy and fun conversations with some new people. How did I manage that, though?

1-over-the-moon::8.title: Over the moon
1-over-the-moon::8.snippetHtml: Probably it’s all of it, all the little things I’ve done to make myself gradually more the sort of person calm enough to just keep moving.

1-over-the-moon::9.title: Over the moon
1-over-the-moon::9.snippetHtml: I don’t know how the Artemis mission will turn out, or if it will even launch today. Nor do I know if I’ll succeed at this new adventure I’ve joined: every day this month, I have to post 500 words or be kicked to the curb.

1-over-the-moon::10.title: Over the moon
1-over-the-moon::10.snippetHtml: I feel confident I can do it. Mostly. Still, there’s nothing that says I cannot fail, consumed in some terrible fire. My confidence says that’s melodrama. It also points out I might be pleasantly surprised by the attention I get.

1-over-the-moon::11.title: Over the moon
1-over-the-moon::11.snippetHtml: Would you take a writer seriously, if they said they weren’t in it for attention? Certainly the pursuit of truth and beauty and justice are worth the words. But how much does it matter, if someone does not read them? Going to the moon without cameras? Absurd!

1-over-the-moon::12.title: Over the moon
1-over-the-moon::12.snippetHtml: So yes, this is about attention. And consistency. And not being overcome by fear. Yet taken off from home, on my comparatively puny mission to learn to better share with you, there are moments I nervously wonder: might I blow up?

2-artificial-and-organic::0.title: The artificial and the organic
2-artificial-and-organic::0.snippetHtml: In the sci-fi novel The Mote in God’s Eye, on making first contact with the Motie species, human experts are baffled at the behaviour of their engineer caste[^1]. They’re savants. Everything they build is bespoke. In place of centralized production lines that spam the Motie masses with millions of the same office chair, they sculpt each seat in the form of its user. When there’s a shift in local needs, the engineers simply decompose and repurpose. The result is an organic infrastructure in which objects are ephemeral but eminently suitable to their niche, and the logistic focus is on the distribution of raw materials rather than finished goods.

2-artificial-and-organic::1.title: The artificial and the organic
2-artificial-and-organic::1.snippetHtml: Even more extreme are Star Trek replicators: you simply describe what you want, then it’s instantly conjured into thinghood in a flurry of sparkles. All that’s needed is a supply of raw, template matter.

2-artificial-and-organic::2.title: The artificial and the organic
2-artificial-and-organic::2.snippetHtml: LLMs have been compared to replicators. It may kind of seem that way, the first few times you use one: you tell it approximately what you want, then sparkles! Products!

2-artificial-and-organic::3.title: The artificial and the organic
2-artificial-and-organic::3.snippetHtml: Use them a few more times, and the dazzle calms down a little. They remain impressive and useful, but you start to notice they’re also idolatrous.[^2] They make idols out of context, worship them, and sometimes try to convince you that you should, too. They need coaxing away from the pretty lights they too easily sit and stare at. Perhaps they aren’t in bad company, then, when their user is so ready to believe they’ve obtained what they feel they wanted.

2-artificial-and-organic::4.title: The artificial and the organic
2-artificial-and-organic::4.snippetHtml: Well, in principle a frontier model might one-shot all sorts of products for you… if you supply exactly the right prompt. This is a Library of Babel sort of situation, where everything is reachable, if you could only pick out the thread that would lead you there. That’s the opposite of bespoke ease, as far as one-shot replication is concerned. Though as you might expect, reality is less extreme than Borges’ story: often the first prompt at least brings us closer to where we want to end up, and to the discerning user, suggests what path to follow next.

2-artificial-and-organic::5.title: The artificial and the organic
2-artificial-and-organic::5.snippetHtml: So the current centaur pairing of user with LLM doesn’t exactly make a replicator, but instead a kind of high-dimensional sculptor. The LLM does the chiseling. The user stands back and says, “Why haven’t you drawn the rest of the owl yet? I asked you to draw an entire owl. And why does it look like it has fur instead of feathers?”.

2-artificial-and-organic::6.title: The artificial and the organic
2-artificial-and-organic::6.snippetHtml: I don’t imagine things will stay like this. Clearly, today’s models can better read between the lines, and make choices more autonomously, than last season’s. But how far do we want to go, inferring wishes and immediately fulfilling them? If some future, all-inferring AI concludes that I’d love the experience machine more than anything, should it just transport me there, sparkling?[^3]

2-artificial-and-organic::7.title: The artificial and the organic
2-artificial-and-organic::7.snippetHtml: No, I don’t think so. I don’t want to short-circuit to the ending. I want the process.[^4] I want to experience, to learn more about myself, and about all of you, and everything. I’d like to see what it’s like to live in an organic civilization, where technology everywhere is eminently suitable to human agency, and doesn’t render it simply irrelevant.

2-artificial-and-organic::8.title: The artificial and the organic
2-artificial-and-organic::8.snippetHtml: Though, of course, could the AI please make an end to the dying and torture and subjugation? Bound us out of the extremes of harm we might bring ourselves to. Then let us get on being our own sculptors for a while.

2-artificial-and-organic::10.title: The artificial and the organic
2-artificial-and-organic::10.snippetHtml: Although the experience of a separate self is illusory, it seems to be a natural stage in the development of consciousness, just like adolescence, or being an infant. You don't look back and go "why was I ever an infant, that was silly, I should have just skipped over that stage".

2-artificial-and-organic::14.snippetHtml: [^1]: Motie castes are more like biological subspecies than human social classes. It’s practically unthinkable for an engineer to be anything else. hashing-python-functions::0.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::0.snippetHtml:
For the past two years, I've developed my machine learning projects with JAX and Equinox. The basis of JAX's power is how flexibly we can compose our computation graphs by writing in a functional paradigm, using transformations like grad, vmap, and jit. But the substance of its power is PyTrees, or the ability to transform over different types of tree-structured inputs in a unified way.

To be clear: "a PyTree" is code for "some nested composition of nodes, which JAX knows how to treat like any other tree because it's been told how to flatten and unflatten the nodes". Technically every Python object is a PyTree, even if it can only be treated as just a single, unstructured leaf.

hashing-python-functions::1.title: Hashing functions by what they select

hashing-python-functions::2.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::2.snippetHtml: A subtree selector function[^1] takes a PyTree, selects one or more nodes, and composes them into some tree to return.

hashing-python-functions::3.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::3.snippetHtml: One use case for subtree selectors is to edit the nodes of a PyTree out-of-place. Suppose we have an instance of some data type:

hashing-python-functions::4.title: Hashing functions by what they select

hashing-python-functions::5.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::5.snippetHtml:
import jax
import equinox as eqx
from equinox import Module

class Foo(Module):
    bar: dict[str, int]
...
hashing-python-functions::5.codeText:
```python
import jax
import equinox as eqx
from equinox import Module

class Foo(Module):
    bar: dict[str, int]
    baz: tuple[float, float]

    def __call__(self, x: jax.Array):
        # If `Foo` were part of a model, we could transform `x` here,
        # using `self.bar` and `self.baz` as parameters.
        ...

tree = Foo(
    dict(a=1, b=2),
    (3.14, 2.718)
)
```

hashing-python-functions::6.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::6.snippetHtml: An Equinox Module is a type of Python dataclass, which JAX can manipulate as a PyTree.

hashing-python-functions::7.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::7.snippetHtml: A selector lets us specify the nodes whose values will be replaced:

hashing-python-functions::8.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::8.snippetHtml:
where_nodes_to_update = lambda tree: (tree.bar['a'], tree.baz)

# Update some parts of the tree
updated_tree = eqx.tree_at(
    where_nodes_to_update,
    tree,
...
hashing-python-functions::8.codeText:
```python
where_nodes_to_update = lambda tree: (tree.bar['a'], tree.baz)

# Update some parts of the tree
updated_tree = eqx.tree_at(
    where_nodes_to_update,
    tree,
    (5, (6.28, 1.618)),
)

updated_tree
>> Foo(bar={'a': 5, 'b': 2}, baz=(6.28, 1.618))
```

hashing-python-functions::9.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::9.snippetHtml:
Similarly, we can use selectors to specify partial initializations of model states. When working with JAX, we typically compose models as trees of Equinox Module objects. Each module node may have leaves which are its parameters; it may also be callable, and specify a transformation of the model state. But to keep the model purely functional, state cannot live inside the modules themselves: it must be passed around separately.

This is the approach I used when designing Feedbax.

hashing-python-functions::10.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::10.snippetHtml: Note: as of March 2026, I no longer use hierarchical state objects/passing, but instead use a dict-like state object, similar to what Equinox uses for stateful operations.

hashing-python-functions::11.title: Hashing functions by what they select

hashing-python-functions::12.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::12.snippetHtml: States typically have default initializations, but users may want to provide custom initializations for some part(s) of the state, without needing to construct the entire PyTree themselves. We might provide the custom initializations as a mapping from selectors, which specify the part(s) of the state to initialize, to the respective data to initialize with.

hashing-python-functions::13.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::13.snippetHtml: Suppose we are given a PyTree of default model states (i.e. arrays), and we'd like to initialize some of its leaves using custom arrays. For each leaf we want to initialize, we could pair its selector with appropriate leaf values to assign to the selected subtree. But maybe we don't know beforehand exactly which leaves we'll want to initialize, so we'd like a general tool that can perform the initialization for us in any case:

hashing-python-functions::14.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::14.snippetHtml:
from collections.abc import Callable
from jaxtyping import Array, PyTree

def replace_nodes(tree: PyTree, spec: Sequence[tuple[Callable, Any]]):
    for where_func, node_value in spec:
        tree = eqx.tree_at(where_func, tree, node_value)
...
hashing-python-functions::14.codeText:
```python
from collections.abc import Callable
from jaxtyping import Array, PyTree

def replace_nodes(tree: PyTree, spec: Sequence[tuple[Callable, Any]]):
    for where_func, node_value in spec:
        tree = eqx.tree_at(where_func, tree, node_value)
    return tree
```

hashing-python-functions::15.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::15.snippetHtml: This works, so long as the structure of the node values matches the structure of their respective selector's return value. However, of course some of our selectors might pick out trees containing redundant leaves from tree, and in that case we'll end up pointlessly replacing the same leaf more than once. Perhaps it is better to assume in this case that our selectors will specify individual, unique leaves (or at least, trees of non-intersecting subsets of leaves). So, suppose instead we use the function:

hashing-python-functions::16.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::16.snippetHtml:
def replace_leaves(tree: PyTree, spec: Sequence[dict[Callable, Any]]):
    for where_func, leaf_value in spec.items():
        tree = eqx.tree_at(where_func, tree, leaf_value)
    return tree

hashing-python-functions::17.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::17.snippetHtml: Now we can specify a mapping between selectors that pick out unique leaves, and the arrays we should replace those leaves with:

hashing-python-functions::18.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::18.snippetHtml:
# Assume these have already been assigned
default_state: PyTree[Array]
some_part_init_data: Array
some_other_init_data: Array

# Construct the mapping from parts of the state PyTree, to the data to initialize them with
...
hashing-python-functions::18.codeText:
```python
# Assume these have already been assigned
default_state: PyTree[Array]
some_part_init_data: Array
some_other_init_data: Array

# Construct the mapping from parts of the state PyTree, to the data to initialize them with
init_state_spec: dict[Callable, Array] = {
    (lambda state: state.some_substate.part): some_part_init_data,
    (lambda state: state.some_other_substate.other_part): some_other_init_data,
}

# Update the default state with the custom init states
initial_state = replace_leaves(default_state, init_state_spec)
```

hashing-python-functions::19.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::19.snippetHtml: This does work, but all is not what it seems. We'll encounter some strange behaviour if we assume that init_state_spec treats its selector keys as unique, because they pick out unique leaves.

hashing-python-functions::20.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::20.snippetHtml: For example, if in some other context we want to determine which data will be used to initialize state.some_substate.part, we might try to access it like so:

hashing-python-functions::21.title: Hashing functions by what they select

hashing-python-functions::22.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::22.snippetHtml: But this doesn't return some_part_init_data! It actually raises a KeyError.

hashing-python-functions::23.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::23.snippetHtml: Likewise, if we already have some init_state_spec and want to update it to use some different data for part of the state, we might try this:

hashing-python-functions::24.title: Hashing functions by what they select

hashing-python-functions::25.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::25.snippetHtml: But this actually adds a new entry to the mapping, rather than replacing the old one.

hashing-python-functions::26.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::26.snippetHtml: What is responsible for this weirdness? Well, Python accesses and assigns dict entries based on the uniqueness of a key's hash... and this doesn't work like you might think, or like I once naively hoped, when the key happens to be a function.

hashing-python-functions::27.title: Hashing functions by what they select

hashing-python-functions::28.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::28.snippetHtml: Any Python object that can be hashed[^2] can be used as a key in a dict. While a Python function is hashable, its hash is based on its object identity, which in CPython (i.e. for almost all Python users) is just its memory address. For example, all of the following expressions evaluate to False:

hashing-python-functions::29.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::29.snippetHtml:
# Explicitly compare by object identity
id(lambda x: x) == id(lambda x: x)
(lambda x: x) is (lambda x: x)

# Implicitly compare by object identity
(lambda x: x) == (lambda x: x)
...
hashing-python-functions::29.codeText:
```python
# Explicitly compare by object identity
id(lambda x: x) == id(lambda x: x)
(lambda x: x) is (lambda x: x)

# Implicitly compare by object identity
(lambda x: x) == (lambda x: x)

# Explicitly compare by hash
hash(lambda x: x) == hash(lambda x: x)
```

hashing-python-functions::30.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::30.snippetHtml: Since these will evaluate False for any function, and since selectors are of course "any function", this example is also False:

hashing-python-functions::31.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::31.codeText:
```python
hash(lambda model: model.some_layer) == hash(lambda model: model.some_layer)
```

hashing-python-functions::32.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::32.snippetHtml: At first this might seem kind of weird. Not only is lambda model: model.some_layer obviously identical to lambda model: model.some_layer in how it's written (i.e. its structure, or syntax), but the two are also obviously identical in how we should expect them to behave (i.e. their meaning, or semantics). Actually, in the case of a subtree selector, syntax and semantics are pretty closely aligned in general: once we know its syntax then we can be pretty certain about what it is going to return, and vice versa, since it's just performing some simple accesses of parts of a data structure.

hashing-python-functions::33.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::33.snippetHtml: If functions were hashed in those terms, then our selectors' uniqueness would be determined just like we want it to be. Seems pretty useful! So why wouldn't Python evaluate hashes or equivalence, in terms of either syntax or semantics?

hashing-python-functions::34.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::34.snippetHtml: Semantics? That's easy. And by "easy", of course I mean impossible: it's a well-known mathematical fact that there's no general method by which we can test whether any two functions will always behave the same way, for all inputs. So if programming language designers want tools like hash and == operators to be general-purpose, and useful for comparing any two functions their users might write, then those tools can't be based on semantic comparisons which are necessarily not general.

hashing-python-functions::35.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::35.snippetHtml: We could also try to evaluate equivalence in terms of syntax, which is the structure of the function's code. This is at least possible, when we have access to the code. But for arbitrary functions it can get expensive: parsing source, building ASTs, and normalizing for trivial differences such as variable names. Perhaps it's enough most of the time to know that two functions aren't literally identical in memory, which is what we test with a direct hash comparison.

hashing-python-functions::36.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::36.snippetHtml: Since dict uses hash to determine the uniqueness of keys, and the hash of a selector is not determined by what it picks out, dict cannot see our selectors the way we see them...

hashing-python-functions::37.title: Hashing functions by what they select

hashing-python-functions::38.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::38.snippetHtml: Once upon a time I decided that I really wanted to be able to use subtree selectors as dict keys. But I knew selectors don't hash in terms of the part(s) of a PyTree they access. So I decided to make a custom type of dict that did not directly (mis)treat them as keys, but instead converted them to an intermediate value which would hash on my terms. For that, I needed a function that takes a selector as input, and returns a hashable representation of its syntax as output.

hashing-python-functions::39.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::39.snippetHtml: I grasped for a function where_func_to_str that would convert a selector to a string. I expected it to behave like so:

hashing-python-functions::40.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::40.codeText:
```python
where_func_to_str(lambda state: state.layer2)
>> "layer2"

where_func_to_str(lambda s: s.some_substate.layer1)
>> "some_substate.layer1"
```

hashing-python-functions::41.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::41.snippetHtml: And maybe I could also get it to work for slightly more complex cases:

hashing-python-functions::42.title: Hashing functions by what they select

hashing-python-functions::43.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::43.snippetHtml: Note that the name of the bound variable ("state", "s", whatever) does not matter here. What is important is that given some PyTree, whatever its name, we are accessing some part(s) of it, whose names are given.

hashing-python-functions::44.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::44.snippetHtml: I hadn't yet imagined how I would handle all possible selectors. For example, this would be no good:

hashing-python-functions::45.title: Hashing functions by what they select

hashing-python-functions::46.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::46.snippetHtml: That's because lists, including ["layer2", "layer3"], aren't hashable. They can't be used as keys! Nor can dicts or sets. Tuples are hashable, so ("layer2", "layer3") is fine as a dict key. Even after we find a where_func_to_str that works like we want, we'll still need to make sure our selectors return PyTrees which are hashable when their leaves are replaced with strings, or else be careful to cast them as such.

hashing-python-functions::47.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::47.snippetHtml: On my quest for a selector-based dict, I made three attempts to write such a where_func_to_str. But before we look at those, let's start with an example that will not work.

hashing-python-functions::48.title: Hashing functions by what they select

hashing-python-functions::49.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::49.snippetHtml: That is, what if we hash the string literal containing the code as it appears in the source file? This is the most direct comparison we can make. It's pretty cheap, since we just need to compare the strings character-by-character until there is a single mismatch. However, it's pretty naive, and hardly useful. Consider that none of the following functions will test as equivalent if we compare them literally, though their differences are trivial:

hashing-python-functions::50.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::50.snippetHtml:
def func(x):
    return x + 1

def func_with_comment(x):
    return x + 1  # ooowee

...

hashing-python-functions::51.title: Hashing functions by what they select

hashing-python-functions::52.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::52.snippetHtml: An Abstract syntax tree (AST) is a data structure specifically intended to represent the syntax of a program. Python's ast implementation would say that all of the functions in the previous example have equivalent ASTs. However it, like most AST implementations, includes the naming of bound variables as part of the syntax. So for example:

hashing-python-functions::53.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::53.snippetHtml:
def compare_ast(*code: str):
    tree_dumps = [ast.dump(ast.parse(s)) for s in code]
    return len(set(tree_dumps)) == 1

compare_ast("lambda x: x", "lambda x: (x)")  # True
compare_ast("lambda x: x", "lambda y: y")  # False; the only difference is a bound variable name
...
hashing-python-functions::53.codeText:
```python
def compare_ast(*code: str):
    tree_dumps = [ast.dump(ast.parse(s)) for s in code]
    return len(set(tree_dumps)) == 1

compare_ast("lambda x: x", "lambda x: (x)")  # True
compare_ast("lambda x: x", "lambda y: y")  # False; the only difference is a bound variable name
```

hashing-python-functions::54.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::54.snippetHtml: There are good reasons why we'd want to preserve bound variable names in ASTs, but when testing for the syntactic equivalence of functions, we generally admit alpha equivalence. Normalizing our ASTs to an alpha-equivalent form can require a little work when dealing with arbitrarily complex functions with nested scopes of bound variables.

hashing-python-functions::55.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::55.snippetHtml: When a programming language designer implements an operator like == for arbitrary comparisons, they don't know how complex the objects to be compared will be. If they base the comparison on structure, then in certain cases a very large amount of work may be implied. Instead, it makes sense to base comparisons on unique ID (e.g. memory address) so that we can tell whether two references are to the same object, while leaving more complex structural comparisons to be implemented by developers on top of the language base.

hashing-python-functions::57.title: Hashing functions by what they select

```python
from collections.abc import Callable
import dis


def get_where_str(where_func: Callable) -> str:
    """
    Returns a string representation of the (nested) attributes accessed by a function.

    Only works for functions that take a single argument, and return that argument,
    or a single (nested) attribute accessed from the argument.
    """
    bytecode = dis.Bytecode(where_func)
    return ".".join(
        instr.argrepr for instr in bytecode
        if instr.opname == "LOAD_ATTR"
    )
```

```python
from collections.abc import Callable
from operator import attrgetter

from jaxtyping import PyTree


def attr_str_tree_to_where_func(tree: PyTree[str, 'T']) -> Callable[[PyTree], PyTree[Any, 'T']]:
    """Reverse transformation to `where_func_to_attr_str_tree`.

    Takes a PyTree of strings describing attribute accesses, and returns a function
    that returns a PyTree of attributes.

    Note: This handles attribute accesses only. Extending to handle item accesses
    (e.g. dict keys, list indices) would require parsing the bracket notation
    from the string representation.
    """
    getters = jt.map(lambda s: attrgetter(s), tree)

    def where_func(obj):
        return jt.map(lambda g: g(obj), getters)

    return where_func
```

```python
from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import TypeVar

import equinox as eqx
import jax.tree as jt
from jax.tree_util import register_pytree_node_class
from jaxtyping import Array, PyTree


T = TypeVar('T')


def _where_to_str(where: Callable) -> str:
    """Return a single string representing an accessor function."""
    terms = where_func_to_attr_str_tree(where)
    if isinstance(terms, str):
        where_str = terms
    else:
        where_str = ", ".join(jt.leaves(terms))
    return where_str

@register_pytree_node_class
class WhereDict(AbstractTransformedOrderedDict[str, Callable[[PyTree], Any], T]):
    """An `OrderedDict` that allows use of accessor functions as keys.

    In particular, keys can be callables (functions/lambdas) that take a single argument,
    and return a PyTree of leaves, as visited by attribute/item accesses.

    Functions are parsed to strings, which can be used interchangeably as keys.
    For example, the following return the same value when `init_spec` is a `WhereDict`:

    > init_spec[lambda state: state.mechanics.effector]
    > init_spec['mechanics.effector']

    Finally, a `tuple[Callable, str]` may also be provided as a key, for cases where
    different unique entries must be included for the same callable. For example,
    the following are equivalent:

    > init_spec[(lambda state: state.mechanics.effector, "first")]
    > init_spec['mechanics.effector#first']

    Note that the hash symbol `#` is used as a delimiter in the string representation.

    ??? Note "Performance"
        For typical initialization mappings (1-10 items) construction is on the order
        of 50x slower than `OrderedDict`. Access is about 2-20x slower, depending
        whether indexed by string or by callable.

        However, we only need to do a single construction and a single access of
        init_spec per batch/evaluation, so performance shouldn't matter too much in
        practice: the added overhead is <50 us/batch, and a batch normally takes
        at least 20,000 us to train.
    """

    def _key_transform(self, key: str | Callable | tuple[Callable, str]) -> str:
        return self.key_transform(key)

    @staticmethod
    def key_transform(key: str | Callable | tuple[Callable, str]) -> str:

        if isinstance(key, str):
            pass
        elif isinstance(key, Callable):
            where_str = _where_to_str(key)
            return where_str
        elif isinstance(key, tuple):
            if not isinstance(key[0], Callable) or not isinstance(key[1], str):
                raise ValueError("Each `WhereDict` key should be supplied as a string, "
                                 "a callable, or a tuple of a callable and a string")
            where_str = _where_to_str(key[0])
            return '#'.join([where_str, key[1]])
        else:
            raise ValueError("Each `WhereDict` key should be supplied as a string, "
                             "a callable, or a tuple of a callable and a string")
        return key

    def __repr__(self):
        return eqx.tree_pformat(self)
```

the-blueberries-of-wrath::43.title: The Blueberries of Wrath
the-blueberries-of-wrath::43.snippetHtml: • Do rodent studies translate to humans? Or even, do results from one transgenic mouse model translate to all mice? These are nagging questions in animal research. At least, the 2018 TH study tests two different mouse types: C57/BL6 mice, which are "normal", and aged A53T mice, which are a model of Parkinson's disease. Additionally, the CREB phosphorylation mechanism by which TH is upregulated is probably conserved across mammals, and we know that both aspirin and dietary salicylates cross into the brain, in humans. But this is not definitive.

the-blueberries-of-wrath::45.title: The Blueberries of Wrath
the-blueberries-of-wrath::45.snippetHtml: • The study shows that aspirin upregulates TH. Does this apply to salicylic acid, and other dietary salicylates? We know that salicylic acid and aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) largely share mechanisms, with a significant exception being aspirin's direct, irreversible COX inhibition which requires the extra acetyl group. More importantly, aspirin is almost entirely metabolized to salicylic acid within 30 minutes or so, and salicylic acid is the substance you'd find circulating in the mice for most of the day after dosing, which makes it more likely that salicylic acid is actually the thing responsible for the upregulation anyway. The study needs to be replicated with salicylic acid, but I bet you'll find a similar effect.

the-blueberries-of-wrath::47.title: The Blueberries of Wrath
the-blueberries-of-wrath::47.snippetHtml: • The dose makes the poison. Assuming dietary salicylates do upregulate TH, how much do I need to consume to do so? The 2018 TH study shows that the TH upregulation happens in a narrow dosage range. So 1 mg or 100 mg of aspirin might not have the same effect, which we might only observe for the dietary salicylate equivalent of around 10 mg of aspirin. The relevant studies are weak (n=20-40 per group) and produced by the same Scottish team [16,17]; one study measured urinary salicyluric acid, and the other, plasma salicylic acid. Their results suggest that vegetarians are similar to people taking 75 mg/day of aspirin, whereas non-vegetarians are perhaps a third of that. Everyone was Scottish and the vegetarians came from a monastery, and we might not expect quite the same results for an average American. But overall these studies roughly accord with expectations, and the equivalent of 10 mg/day probably accounts for a non-negligible subset of most populations.

the-blueberries-of-wrath::49.snippetHtml: On the off-chance that this "salicylate and/or polyphenols cause too much PFC dopamine and thus rumination" hypothesis is actually relevant, one of its strengths is that it would validate that some people do experience adverse effects from fruit, while also potentially explaining why they are so fixated on whatever explanations they can scrounge up to clothe their miseries. Of course, other mechanisms may still contribute in parallel.[^8]

the-blueberries-of-wrath::50.title: The Blueberries of Wrath
the-blueberries-of-wrath::50.snippetHtml: This post was a speculative review of potential mechanisms. As we just saw, there's plenty of uncertainty remaining around methodology, mechanisms, and dosing. I'll finish with a couple of general issues we haven't covered yet.

the-blueberries-of-wrath::51.title: The Blueberries of Wrath
the-blueberries-of-wrath::51.snippetHtml: First, there are significant differences in salicylate content for each specific food source. We should assume that a blueberry will contain different levels of specific salicylates and polyphenols depending on growing conditions, cultivars, regions, and estimation methods.

the-blueberries-of-wrath::52.title: The Blueberries of Wrath
the-blueberries-of-wrath::52.snippetHtml: Second, leaving aside concerns about mechanism and replication, probably the greatest source of variability remaining is the absorption and distribution of dietary substances, especially polyphenols. Many polyphenols have low bioavailability[^7], especially because they are actively yeeted back out of the intestinal wall by the bouncer (P-glycoprotein) right after absorption.[^6] Likewise, many polyphenols act as prebiotics for gut microbes, and it might be the metabolites that are actually relevant here, and which would need to be assayed in vivo if we wanted to be thorough about it.

the-blueberries-of-wrath::53.title: The Blueberries of Wrath
the-blueberries-of-wrath::53.snippetHtml: Well, there it is. Are you afraid yet? You shouldn't be. Fruit is probably mostly fine for you.

the-blueberries-of-wrath::54.title: The Blueberries of Wrath
the-blueberries-of-wrath::54.snippetHtml: [^0]: I won't be covering the fructose question here, but I don't think there's any clear evidence against fructose intake from fruit, even though large enough boluses of plain fructose are known to be harmful to gut microbiome and liver metabolism. For sedentary individuals, anyway. [^1]: "Salicylates" includes the drug aspirin, a.k.a. acetylsalicylic acid. Aspirin in particular is dangerous to give to children, as it can cause Reye's syndrome, but this is probably specific to aspirin and there's no evidence to suggest it applies to dietary salicylates. [^2]: There are two active forms of COX, COX-1 and COX-2. Different NSAIDs have different selectivity for one or the other. Aspirin prefers COX-1, especially at low doses. Naproxen is about equally balanced. Ibuprofen slightly prefers COX-2. Diclofenac and all the drugs in the coxib family are COX-2 selective. COX-1 inhibition is antithrombotic (by reducing production of thromboxane A2) but is also largely responsible for negative effects of NSAIDs on the gut, which is why aspirin is the most cardioprotective but also the most stomach-melting of the bunch. COX-2 inhibition is primarily anti-inflammatory, and while the absence of COX-1 inhibition by coxibs means they are comparatively gut-safe, it is also pro-thrombotic (due to reducing production of prostacyclin while sparing thromboxane A2) and thus increases the risk of cardiovascular adverse events with chronic use. [^3]: There are several clues why:

the-blueberries-of-wrath::63.title: The Blueberries of Wrath
the-blueberries-of-wrath::63.snippetHtml: This all points to a pathological attractor state; a self-reinforcing equilibrium in the system dynamics. It's uncertain which of these doors leads to the attractor in the first place. It does seem it's not strictly congenital, but tends to arise in a patient's 30s or 40s following a severe upper respiratory infection, suggesting an epigenetic trigger.

the-blueberries-of-wrath::64.title: The Blueberries of Wrath
the-blueberries-of-wrath::64.snippetHtml: [^4]: Salicylic acid is similarly anti-inflammatory to aspirin, but probably by a combination of different upstream mechanisms, such as inhibition of IκB kinase β → less NF-κB production, and less downstream upregulation of COX-2 conditional on being in an inflammatory state. But ultimately aspirin shares these mechanisms, as it's partly metabolized to salicylic acid. [^5]: Plants contain other substances which might be relevant (but probably aren't):

the-blueberries-of-wrath::65.title: The Blueberries of Wrath
the-blueberries-of-wrath::65.snippetHtml: • Several polyphenols inhibit 5-LOX in vitro. A very weak (n=11, uncontrolled, 4-week longitudinal) pilot study [14] showed decreased 5-LOX activation and reduced production of leukotrienes by eosinophils, in participants consuming 100 mg/day of soy isoflavones for 4 weeks. A later, stronger RCT (n=386, placebo-controlled, 24 weeks) [15] returned a negative result for asthma measures, even after verifying that the crucial isoflavone genistein was present at plasma levels sufficient to match in vitro inhibition conditions, suggesting either that the polyphenol was not entering eosinophils from plasma, or else that 5-LOX inhibition is inadequate to control asthma. And anyway, 100 mg/day of isoflavones is equivalent to about a pound of tofu, or 5-10 cups of soy milk.

the-blueberries-of-wrath::67.title: The Blueberries of Wrath
the-blueberries-of-wrath::67.snippetHtml: • Some polyphenols inhibit the enzyme COMT, which metabolizes catechols (dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine, and others). This could increase the half-life of circulating epinephrine → activates β2 adrenergic receptors in the lungs → dilates airways, by the same mechanism as asthma medications like salbutamol. As far as I can see this has not been tested, but I doubt it is significant as there are other mechanisms for clearing plasma epinephrine which should pick up the slack.

the-blueberries-of-wrath::73.title: The Blueberries of Wrath
the-blueberries-of-wrath::73.snippetHtml: [^6]: P-glycoprotein serves a similar role at the blood-brain barrier, bouncing things back out. This is why loperamide, an opioid, treats diarrhea but does not get you high, and also why the antihistamine cetirizine makes you less drowsy than diphenhydramine. We expect variability here for a few reasons: 1) P-glycoprotein has different affinity for different substrates, as usual, 2) P-glycoprotein expression varies between individuals, and 3) P-glycoprotein is inhibited by certain dietary substances, such as piperine from black pepper. [^7]: In the case of quercetin, for example, we need to reach 1-8 µM to effectively inhibit COMT [8], but usually we can only get 0.1-0.2 µM in plasma. [^8]: One example that's close to the kind of salicylate sensitivity seen in AERD involves brain mast cells: though there are few of them, if they were in an AERD-like hypersensitive state, we might expect salicylates to cause them to activate, with downstream psychiatric effects. [^9]: This is sometimes called the inverted-U model of prefrontal dopamine [19].
